paras: The attempted lynching of William Stock took place in Kansas City, Missouri, on March 29, 1882, when about one thousand friends of a man shot dead in Stock's West Kansas City saloon tried to lynch Stock after his capture. Officers got the prisoner into jail, where he was reported safely confined. The story ran as a short wire item, and one printing gave the prisoner's name as "William Mack".

According to a National Associated Press dispatch dated March 28, Martin Monahan and Jerry Folley were in a saloon kept by Wm. Stock at about nine that night, arguing over who should be elected councilman from their ward. In that account Monahan and Folley struck Stock, who hit Monahan on the head with a pistol, and in the fight that followed Stock fired three shots, killing Monahan and slightly wounding Folley. A separate wire paragraph called Stock "a bully" who had killed a man at a Chicago race track a few years before and placed the "political row" in Kansas City, Kansas.

Stock was captured in Kansas on March 29, in the morning according to one printing of the dispatch and in the evening according to another. About one thousand men gathered and tried to lynch the prisoner, and the Omaha Bee's version identified them as "Monohan's friends." The officers "succeeded in grabbing him" and lodged him in jail. The dispatch does not say where the crowd met the officers or whether anyone was hurt.
No later report of an inquest into Monahan's death, a trial of Stock, or any arrest of crowd members was found in the coverage.

The episode reached distant papers only through brief telegraph items. On March 29 the Omaha Daily Bee printed the account of the saloon fight, and the Rock Island Argus ran the shorter "bully" paragraph among other "Shooting Affrays"; the St. Paul Daily Globe reprinted that paragraph the next day as "Wm. S. Lack." On March 30 the New Haven Morning Journal and Courier headed the capture dispatch "Arrest of a Murderer," while the Omaha Bee headed it "Murderer Caught."
Both versions called the prisoner a murderer before any trial and gave the lynching attempt a single sentence, with no comment on the crowd. None of the reports mentioned the race of anyone involved.

The New Haven printing named the prisoner "William Mack" and said the crowd were "his friends," while the otherwise identical Omaha printing named him William Stock and said they were Monahan's friends. Because the original account of the shooting and the separate wire paragraph also name Stock, "Mack" appears to be a transmission error. The papers also differ on Monahan's first name, Martin in the shooting reports and Mike in the capture dispatch.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of William Stock
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
bases: A crowd of about one thousand tried to lynch a man arrested for a saloon killing, and officers kept him from them and jailed him (A4, A5); no paper gives anyone's race, and the shooting came out of a fight over a ward election (A2, A3).
The crowd of about one thousand acted without legal authority over an accused killing, but officers got the prisoner into jail and no one was killed (A4, A5); this was an attempted lynching.

Two printings of the Kansas City wire (A4, A5) agree on the capture, the crowd of about one thousand and the jailing, and two separate earlier dispatches (A2, A3) report the shooting; they differ on the shooter's name and on whose friends formed the crowd.

framing.detail: Headed 'Arrest of a Murderer' and 'Murderer Caught', the items call the prisoner a murderer and report the lynching attempt in one sentence, with no comment.

A5 names the dead man's friends, which fits an attempted lynching; A4's 'his' is ambiguous rather than contradictory.

info: Monahan was shot about 9 p.m. on March 28, 1882; the shooter was captured and the crowd tried to lynch him on March 29, 1882.
The shooting was in a saloon kept by Stock in West Kansas City; the shooter was captured 'in Kansas' and jailed at Kansas City.
The man the crowd tried to lynch: the saloon keeper named William (Wm.) Stock in A2, A3 and A5, 'William Mack' in A4; race not stated.
Accused of shooting and killing Martin (Mike) Monahan and wounding Jerry Folley in his saloon during a quarrel over who should be elected councilman from their ward.
Friends of the dead man ('Monohan's friends' in A5; 'his friends' in A4).
The prisoner was 'safely confined' in jail; no later report was found.
